I.          Introduction

[
1
]

On or about October 11, 2013 Glenn Winningham Fearn
had an incident entering the Canadian border. He was detained and arrested by
officers of the Canada Border Services Agency [the “CBSA”]. That incident resulted
in weapons charges laid against the Petitioner. Those charges are currently in
the Provincial Court [the “Border Action”] where the presiding Judge entered a
not guilty plea on behalf of the Petitioner. Trial is scheduled for March 3-6,
2014.

[
2
]

Mr. Fearn is a litigant who employs Organized
Pseudolegal Commercial Argument [“OPCA”] concepts and schemes. The OPCA
phenomenon and case law that comments on this subject were comprehensively
reviewed in a recent decision of this court,
Meads v Meads
,
2012
ABQB 571
, 543 AR 215 [“
Meads
”]. In brief, these are
legal-sounding techniques that allegedly permit persons to avoid practically
any obligation from income tax to child support payments, ‘opt out’ of
government control, unilaterally define what is the law, set fines for conduct
an individual does not like, and pay bills out of secret “birth bond” bank
accounts.

[
3
]

OPCA schemes never work. OPCA concepts are no
more than flights of conspiratorial fancy and wish fulfillment. Sadly,
individuals who employ OPCA techniques [“OPCA litigants”] are two-fold victims:
first of their own imprudence, and second to the conmen who market these
schemes on a commercial basis to the desperate, foolish, and greedy.

[
4
]

Meads v Meads
investigates and responds to OPCA schemes in a largely civil
context; in that case a man, Dennis Larry Meads, unsuccessfully employed a
range of OPCA schemes in an attempt to avoid his child and spousal support
obligations. Mr. Fearn arrives in this court in a very different fashion: he is
the subject of a criminal proceeding. Mr. Fearn’s extensive argument and
material not only provides an opportunity to evaluate the futility of OPCA
concepts as a defence against a criminal prosecution, but permits this Court to
develop a schematic approach to two subjects which were not addressed in
Meads
:

1.
Can OPCA litigation in a criminal law context warrant costs, and if so, when?

2.         How does the law of contempt of court respond to OPCA
ideas, pseudolegal arguments, and the commercial context in which this material
is propagated?

[
5
]

The issue of contempt arises in a number of
ways, but first as a result of Mr. Fearn’s written submissions, which attack
state and judicial authority and persons in a manner that straddles the line
between revolutionary rhetoric and hostility-speech.  This is also not Mr.
Fearn’s first litigation in Canada; he has a history of this kind of speech and
allegations. Mr. Fearn is affiliated with a US OPCA movement, the Sovereign
Citizens/Men, who have a troubling history of moving past words to illegal and
violent action. This too is reflected in what Mr. Fearn said in court, and
wrote in his documentary submissions.

II.        Mr.
Fearn’s Application

[
6
]

This Queen’s Bench application is Mr. Fearn’s attempt
to halt the Provincial Court proceedings. He advances a number of alternative
remedies this Court is asked to consider and grant. The application is best
described as unorthodox, and was supported by a large volume of materials, most
in a document titled “Notice of Objection and Non-Consent to your Roman Civil Law
by Affidavit” [the “Notice”], which attached and referenced many lengthy items.

[
7
]

The Crown counters that Mr. Fearn’s arguments
are

1.         legally incorrect Organized Pseudolegal Commercial
Argument schemes, as defined in
Meads
,

2.         a
collateral attack upon the Provincial Court proceeding, and

3.         otherwise
legally or procedurally incorrect, or defective in form.

The Crown requested Mr. Fearn’s
future filing with the Court be restricted and an award of costs made in response
to this inappropriate application.

[
8
]

This matter raises four general issues:

1.         Should
Mr. Fearn receive the remedies he seeks?

2.         Whether Mr. Fearn’s access to the court should be
restricted, and if so, in what manner?

3.         Should costs be ordered against Mr. Fearn in the event
his application is unsuccessful?

4.         What other court response or responses are appropriate to
Mr. Fearn’s litigation, documents, and in-court statements?

[
9
]

I will not review the substance of Mr. Fearn’s
alleged Oct. 11, 2013 misconduct as that is immaterial to this proceeding, and
is instead the subject of the Border Action in the Provincial Court.

[
10
]

Mr. Fearn identifies himself in a number of
different ways: Glenn Winningham, Glenn Winningham Fearn, Glenn Winningham of
the House of Fearn. My understanding is that his actual name is Glenn
Winningham Fearn, and I shall refer to him on that basis. I note that the “House
of” variation of his name is legally meaningless:
R v Sargent
,
2004
ONCJ 356
at para
29
, [2005] 1 CTC 448;
Meads
, at paras
209-210
.

[
11
]

Mr. Fearn’s application was heard and rejected
on January 13, 2014. I declined to award costs, but restricted Mr. Fearn’s
right to file further materials in the Court of Queen’s Bench. On that date I
reserved the option to provide these further and more detailed reasons.

A.        The Application

[
12
]

Speaking broadly, Mr. Fearn seeks to have this
Court end the Border Action against him in Provincial Court. He expresses this
remedy in a number of ways:

1.         An
Order of Prohibition against Canada Customs [in the Border Action].

2.         An Order vacating the decisions made by Canada Customs on
11 October 2013, when they unlawfully arrested the Petitioner, and all
subsequent orders and decisions, as void, and a nullity.

3.         An
Order of Non-Suit ... [in the Border Action].

4.         An
Order staying the [Border Action proceedings].

[
13
]

Mr. Fearn also seeks compensation for alleged
misconduct by government actors:

5.         An Order that the Petitioner be compensated for the false
imprisonment that resulted from their void decisions, judgments, and orders,
and the malicious prosecution that continues to this day.

[
14
]

During the oral hearing Mr. Fearn also indicated
that he intends to seek damages from certain Crown and court actors, but that
will occur via other separate litigation.

B.        Grounds for the Application

[
15
]

In his written application Mr. Fearn said the
basis for his litigation was:

1.         He
filed a lawsuit in 2010 challenging Canada Customs jurisdiction in Lethbridge
Court of Queen’s Bench ...;

2.         When
the Petitioner cross [sic] the so-called border, Customs knew who he was
because they had him listed as “armed and dangerous” in their system;

3.         Canada
Customs knew about the lawsuit because they brought it up, in the first
hearing;

4.         Canada
Customs has done nothing to prove their Roman Civil Law Statutory jurisdiction,
except bring out their guns, and assault the Petitioner, and kidnap the
Petitioner, and falsely imprison the Petitioner;

5.         The
decision/judgment made by Canada Customs is void and an absolute nullity.

...

The 2010 lawsuit identified above
by Mr. Fearn is
Winningham v Canada
(30 November 2010) Lethbridge
1006 00907 (Alta QB), leave to appeal denied (Alta CA).

[
16
]

The Notice and Mr. Fearn’s oral arguments expands
on this list of alleged grounds to end the Border Action, and other claims of
court and state misconduct.

C.        The Crown’s Response

[
17
]

Mr. Benkendorf, on behalf of the federal Crown,
argues Mr. Fearn is clearly a litigant who advances OPCA arguments, as surveyed
and distilled in Associate Chief Justice Rooke’s decision in
Meads
.

On top of that, he is the representative Sovereign Citizen/Man litigant
actually
referred to

by name
in
Meads
, see paras
176, 178
.

[
18
]

The Crown asks Mr. Fearn’s petition be struck,
because:

1.
Prohibition

is not appropriate regarding a Provincial Court Proceeding;

2.
Vacating a Decision
made by Canada Customs should
be in front of the proper Court, which in this case is Federal Court;

3.
Non-suits
are typically an issue for trial based
on evidence (or lack of it) - which is not this case;

4.
The Stay
has not been appropriately argued per the
tripartite test typical of such applications; and

5.
Compensation
for False Imprisonment – again, this
is premature because,
inter alia
, there is no verdict in the Provincial
Court weapons proceedings.

[
19
]

I anticipate
Meads
and these reasons
may be potentially instructive if the hypothetical litigation in Federal Court
were to occur.

III.       Analysis

[
20
]

The legal analysis in this decision has two
general parts: first I will examine whether Mr. Fearn’s application should be
granted or refused. Second, I will continue to evaluate what other, collateral
responses may be appropriate to this application: costs, and whether Mr. Fearn
has engaged in contempt of court.

[
21
]

The first step is therefore to evaluate Mr.
Fearn’s application and his arguments. My summary of the lengthy written grounds
advanced by Mr. Fearn in his oral arguments are as follows:

1.         CBSA
and Canadian customs are criminals; they violate due process;

2.         he wants damages against Customs,
inter alia,
because
he is sick and tired of the way he is treated at the border;

3.         he
believes the CBSA acted under colour of law and otherwise without authority;

4.         he challenges the Provincial Court’s jurisdiction and
wants its proceedings stopped;

5.         certain legislation is “pretend legislation” and has no
legal effect;

6.         he could use lethal force against Customs Officer agents
if they arrest him unlawfully;

7.         the
Alberta Court of Appeal “sold their justice” in his prior appeal; and

8.         he
may yet file another Statement of Claim for damages.

Again, if Mr. Fearn were to proceed
with one or more further lawsuits that claimed damages then
Meads

and this decision may be relevant.

[
22
]

Mr. Fearn also makes broad allegations of
conspiracy and misconduct by government officials and judges at all three
levels of Alberta courts
.
In addition, Mr. Fearn has demanded the oaths
of office for certain Queen’s Bench Justices and has unsuccessfully sought the
same from Wittmann, CJ. Mr. Fearn says he requires these oaths to evaluate
whether these persons are properly authorized.

[
23
]

Apparently, Mr. Fearn has or will file criminal
complaints including proceedings against the Alberta Court of Appeal, Wittmann
CJ, and Langston J, and others
.
He, at the hearing, indicates he also
plans to initiate other legal actions against these and other judges.

[
24
]

Mr. Fearn’s materials and argument ranged
through many and varied topics. I reject his application on three bases:

1.         this
application offends the rule against collateral attack,

2.         the alleged range of defects to Crown and court authority
are legally incorrect, and

3.         Mr.
Fearn’s application is otherwise frivolous and vexatious.

[
25
]

I also generally accept the Crown arguments that
the orders sought for a non-suit, to vacate a decision, and for compensation
are in the incorrect forum or format. A non-suit application (or more properly
a directed verdict) may be made at the close of the Crown case in the Border
Action, not here. Mr. Fearn’s challenge to the actions of Canada Customs would
be properly made in the Federal Court as a judicial review (
Federal Courts
Act
, RSC 1985, c F-7, ss 18-18.1), though I agree with Mr. Benkendorf’s
suggestion that Court would also refuse to take any step until the Border
Action was concluded.

[
26
]

Mr. Fearn’s claim for compensation is equally
defective. This application is not a legal action such as a tort lawsuit that
permits that kind of award, nor has Mr. Fearn requested financial compensation
as a s 24(1) remedy for a breach of his rights under the
Canadian Charter of
Rights and Freedoms
, Part 1,
Constitution Act, 1982
, being Schedule
B to the
Canada Act 1982 (UK)
, 1982, c 11 [the “
Charter
”].

[
27
]

I will first address the issue of collateral
attack.

A.        Collateral Attack

[
28
]

Claiming his status as “sovereign” and on an
unrealistic reading of common law and civil law, Mr. Fearn’s application cites
centuries old law, ranging back to the
Magna Carta
and ancient Roman
Law. However, this Court and other Canadian courts apply another principle of
law that strongly establishes rules that a Court cannot review or vary the
decision of another court except in the proper procedural context, such as an
appeal.

[
29
]

Any attempt to litigate outside of that context
is a “collateral attack”, as was recently explained by Justice Abella in
British
Columbia (Workers’ Compensation Board) v Figliola
,
2011 SCC 52
, at para

28
, [2011] 3 SCR 422:

The rule against collateral attack similarly
attempts to protect the fairness and integrity of the justice system by
preventing duplicative proceedings.
It prevents a party from using an
institutional detour to attack the validity of an order by seeking a different
result from a different forum, rather than through the designated appellate or
judicial review route
… [Emphasis added.]

See also:
R v Litchfield
,

1993 CanLII 44 (SCC)
, [1993] 4 SCR 333, 86 CCC (3d) 97;
Quebec (Attorney General) v Laroche
,

2002 SCC 72
, 219 DLR (4th) 723;
R v Sarson
,
1996 CanLII 200 (SCC)
, [1996] 2 SCR
223, 135 DLR (4th) 402.

[
30
]

Courts have held firm to this principle for over
100 years: see
Clark v Phinney
(1896),
1896 CanLII 74 (SCC)
, 25 SCR 633 at 642-624, and
other cases as cited in
R v Wilson
,
1983 CanLII 35 (SCC)
, [1983] 2 SCR 594, 4 DLR (4th)
577.

[
31
]

Mr. Fearn’s correct course of action is to
complete the Border Action in provincial court, and if he is dissatisfied with
the result, he may then appeal. The remedy that Mr. Fearn seeks, an order of
prohibition, is an exceptional judicial review remedy. Mr. Fearn has provides neither
a legal basis to establish either a lack of court jurisdiction (that discussion
follows later in this decision) or the kinds of prejudice discussed in
decisions such as
R v Hill
,
2011 ONSC 3935
, 107 OR (3d) 40;
R
v Prigotzke
,
2005 ABQB 653
, 66 WCB (2d) 682; and
R v Anson

(1983),
1983 CanLII 284 (BC CA)
, 146 DLR (3d) 661, 42 BCLR 282 (BCCA).

[
32
]

Further, intervention by this court in that
manner is strictly at the discretion of the reviewing court (
R v Anson
,
at para
22
), and I agree with Watson J (as he then was) that “criminal justice
should not be a fragmentary process, with parties oscillating between court
levels.”:
R v Song
,
2001 ABQB 689
, 296 AR 132. In other words, Mr.
Fearn’s application for prohibition is therefore inappropriate and premature as
a collateral attack on the Provincial Court proceeding.

[
33
]

Similarly, Mr. Fearn’s argument for a stay is
denied, and in any case he has not met his onus to prove the three criteria for
a stay identified in
RJR - MacDonald Inc. v Canada (Attorney General)
,

1994 CanLII 117 (SCC)
, [1994] 1 SCR 311, 111 DLR (4th) 385 on a balance of probabilities. In fact, his
stay application fails on the first step, which requires Mr. Fearn’s
application has a basis in law, and is not frivolous or vexatious. These
deficiencies are detailed below.

B.        Specific OPCA Arguments

[
34
]

Beyond offending the rule against collateral
attack with his premature application, Mr. Fearn is wrong on a great many specific
points. His allegations, argument, and materials appear to in many instances entwine
incompatible perspectives, archaic, obsolete, or foreign legal authorities, and
are a distorted and an exaggerated image of the law. He is incorrect in his
legal history, legal principle, and legal procedure. Thus, since his arguments
were “all over the map,” it is possible my analysis of his claims is potentially
incomplete. Nevertheless, I believe I have dissected out the majority of
distinct points on which I can comment and then provide the legal basis for why
Mr. Fearns’s arguments are so singularly miscounseled.

[
35
]

Though otherwise amorphous, Mr. Fearn’s argument
has a central theme: he is, by some mechanism, outside the authority of the
CBSA and Alberta courts. In the Notice he accepts the authority of this court
only

for his desired purposes and
none other
:

... I do NOT consent to the jurisdiction of
this so-called Court other than for the Order of Prohibition, that is demanded ...

As will later become apparent, the
tone of this statement is not an isolated anomaly.

[
36
]

His oral argument repeats this position:

… do me a favour, do us both a favour, I
don’t want to be here, if you’re going to try and make me your slave, I don’t
want to be here and – and so – so I have a right to be left alone, you know,
and this continual harassment is – is unacceptable, and that’s the bottom line
and – and quite frankly, you know … it’s your job to protect my rights, you
know, I mean really, if you think about it.

[
37
]

As for the CBSA, Mr. Fearn argued they had no
authority at all over him:

Once they find out that I’m – I am who I am,
they should say have a nice day. They can stop foreigners, and that’s it.

[
38
]

In contrast Mr. Fearn says his application is
simply no more than due process, and he is entitled to that.

[
39
]

I will not detail the various authorities that
Mr. Fearn cites for his arguments. These are a hodgepodge of Bible quotes, case
law, much of it American and dating to the 19
th
century, quotes from
archaic legal dictionaries, and legal texts, both modern and ancient. Other
sources are dark and conspiratorial. The documents attached to the Notice,
which also appear created by Mr. Fearn, share the Notice’s dubious foundation.

[
40
]

These authorities are of little relevance, and
instead their character and effect is captured by the conclusion of Justice
Myers in
R v Porisky
,
2012 BCSC 67
, [2012] 4 CTC 160:

Mr. Porisky’s analysis picks and chooses
snippets from various statutes and cases, and attempts to create logical links
where none exist.  It is, in effect, legal numerology.

[
41
]

Readers interested in the authorities identified
in Mr. Fearn’s scheme should refer to Appendix A which reproduces parts of the
Notice.

1.         The Provincial Court
Judge Had No Authority to Make a Guilty Plea

[
42
]

Mr. Fearn complains that at the Dec. 17, 2013
hearing Judge Hironaka entered a plea of “not guilty” on his behalf:

It was a not guilty plea, but – but I
haven’t consented to this jurisdiction from the beginning, I’ve been
challenging it for three years or longer, and so by them taking jurisdiction
and entering a plea, that’s admitting jurisdiction and – and I don’t consent to
that jurisdiction ...

... that’s a void judgment because they
didn’t have jurisdiction, I never gave them jurisdiction, I’ve been challenging
jurisdiction for years.

[
43
]

Judge Hironaka made no error when he took this
step. He conformed to the procedure set by
Criminal Code
, s 606(2):

606(2)  Where
an accused refuses to plead or does not answer directly, the court shall order
the clerk of the court to enter a plea of not guilty.

This process is a routine feature
of criminal proceedings in Canada, for example:
R v Leibel
,

2000 SKQB 565
at para
58
, 202 SaskR 206;
R v Lemieux
,
2007 SKPC
135
at para
19
, [2008] 2 CTC 291;
R v Greenlaw
,
1968 CanLII 144
at p 2 (NBCA).

[
44
]

Detaxer guru David Kevin Lindsay advanced a more sophisticated
variation of this same argument in
R v Lindsay
,
2011 BCCA 99
at
paras
11-20
, 302 BCAC 76, leave refused [2011] SCCA No 265, where Lindsay
argued he was not a “person” and therefore fell outside the court’s authority.
He, a “non-person”, then refused to plead either not guilty or guilty. The
British Columbia Court of Appeal concluded that the order to enter a plea of
not guilty indicated the trial court had implicitly found it had jurisdiction
to hear the matter, and that the trial judge had been correct in coming to that
conclusion.

[
45
]

As this decision shows I confirm that implicit finding by the
Provincial Court judge. Mr. Fearn’s argument on this basis is therefore
rejected. Mr. Fearn’s remedy is to appeal, after the final decision in
Provincial Court, that decision by the trial judge to take jurisdiction, as
occurred in
R v Lindsay
.

2.         The Applicable Law

[
46
]

Mr. Fearn makes a broad and rather ill-defined
distinction between the categories of law that do and do not apply to him. He
indicates that the CBSA and courts are acting under the later kind of law. He
divides law up into a number of types or forms, though their definition and scope
appears more to be a matter of convenience than schematic.

[
47
]

This concept re-appears in various forms in his
oral argument and the Notice:

•

Mr. Fearn is a “sovereign living soul”, and has
put himself into “common law” rather than a “Roman civil law jurisdiction”;

•

the
Magna Carta
is common law and applies
to him;

•

Mr. Fearn has a “right under natural law to be
left alone”;

•

the state actors and the court apply “Roman
civil law”;

•

a detention is “military law”, and he did not
consent “… to any military jurisdiction”; and

•

he is not subject to the
Charter of Rights
and Freedoms
, that is only for “federal citizens”.

[
48
]

Mr. Fearn also uses these categories of law to
explain why the
Meads
judgment is irrelevant to him and this
action:

… the case Meads v. Meads is a divorce
proceeding, which is clearly not common law, okay, that’s – that’s nothing to
do with common law, that’s equity and admiralty, and it has nothing to do with
common law, and so, you know, all of that stuff, in an admiralty court, you
know, that’s – that’s perfectly appropriate in an admiralty or equity court.
I’m not interested in dealing with – and that’s all Roman civil law.

[
49
]

It appears Mr. Fearn believes that he is subject
to kinds of law other than “common law” only if he
consents
to application
of that law. To avoid that result he has filed with government and court
authorities documents called an “Objection and Non-Consent to Roman Civil Law”
that ‘estop’ action against him under that category of law. He asks “Where’s
the contract?” that would establish consent. Without his consent, he argues, the
CBSA’s actions were therefore assault, unlawful arrest, kidnapping, false
imprisonment, and unlawful search and seizure of Mr. Fearn’s property. The CBSA
and Provincial Court acted “under a colour of law and has no authority.”

[
50
]

Mr. Fearn’s schema of law is unorthodox and in
no way reflects the historical development of Commonwealth legal traditions,
jurisprudence, or academic discourse. His perspective could just as easily and
accurately be expressed in this way:

1.         There is a kind of law that I like, which are my own
rules, which I call common law. It applies to me.

2.         There
are many other kinds of law but they don’t apply to me, because I say so.

[
51
]

A fundamental misunderstanding of the term
“common law” runs throughout much of the OPCA world. Mr. Fearn appears to be
one such subscriber. This “mutant” version of the common law is discussed in
detail by Associate Chief Justice Rooke in
Meads
at paras
326-327
:

[326]  It is helpful at this point to make a
few comments on the manner in which OPCA litigants often use the term “common
law”. OPCA litigants often draw an arbitrary line between “statutes” and
“common law”, and say they are subject to “common law”, but not legislation. Of
course, the opposite is in fact true, the “common law” is law developed
incrementally by courts, and which is subordinate to legislation: statutes and
regulations passed by the national and provincial governments. The Constitution
Act provides the rules and principles that restrict the scope and nature of
legislation, both by jurisdiction and on the basis of rights (ie. the
Charter
).

[327]  Persons who claim to only be subject

2011 ABQB 11

at para

,

2008 ABQB 472
at para
21
, 453 AR 337.

[
96
]

frivolous.”:
Maxwell et al v John W. Snow and the US Department of
Treasury,
409

F 3d 354 (May 27, 2005, US Ct of Appeals DC
circuit). Similarly, for those who believe they are sovereigns and not subject

US
v Greenstreet
, 912 F supp 224 (ND Tex 1996).

[
97
]

Wong v Leung
,
2011 ABQB 688
at para
33
, 530 AR
82;
Mcmeekin v Alberta (Attorney General)
,
2012 ABQB 144
at para

11
, 537 AR 136. In
R v Scott
,
1990 CanLII 27 (SCC)
, [1990] 3 SCR 979 at 1007, 116 NR
361 McLachlin J (as she then was) observed:

... abuse of process may be established
where: (1) the proceedings are oppressive or vexatious; and, (2) violate the
fundamental principles of justice underlying the community's sense of fair play
and decency. The concepts of oppressiveness and vexatiousness underline the

[
98
]

Reece v Edmonton (City)
,
2011 ABCA 238
at
para
14

2.         Restriction of
Vexatious Litigants

[
99
]

A court-ordered end to litigation is not the
only response available to address the deleterious effects of frivolous or
vexatious litigation. The
Judicature Act
, RSA 2000, c J-2, ss 23-23.1
permits court-ordered restrictions on the ability of a person who engages in
“vexatious” litigation to initiate or continue litigation in Alberta courts. Vexatious
conduct is defined in s 23(2):

23(2)    For the purposes of this Part,
instituting
vexatious proceedings or conducting a proceeding in a vexatious
manner includes
, without limitation,
any one
or more of the
following:

(a)
persistently
bringing proceedings to determine an issue that has already been determined by
a court of competent jurisdiction
;

(b)
persistently
bringing proceedings that cannot succeed or that have no reasonable expectation
of providing relief
;

(c)
persistently
bringing proceedings for improper purposes
;

(d)
persistently
using previously raised grounds and issues in subsequent proceedings
inappropriately
;

(e)        persistently
failing to pay the costs of unsuccessful proceedings on the part of the person
who commenced those proceedings;

(f)
persistently
taking unsuccessful appeals from judicial decisions
;

(g)        persistently
engaging in inappropriate courtroom behaviour.

[Emphasis
added.]

[
100
]

The decision of
Dykun v Odinshaw
,

2000 ABQB 548
at para
42
, 267 AR 318, affirmed
2001 ABCA 204
, 286 AR 392,
leave denied [2001] SCCA No 442 provides a largely parallel set of indicia of
vexatious conduct. A proceeding is vexatious if it satisfies
any
of the
following tests:

(a) the
bringing of one or more actions to determine an issue which has already been
determined by a court of competent jurisdiction constitutes a vexatious proceeding;

(b) where
it is obvious that an action cannot succeed, or if the action would lead to no
possible good, or if no reasonable person can reasonably expect to obtain relief,
the action is vexatious;

(c)
vexatious actions include those brought for an improper purpose, including the
harassment and oppression of other parties by multifarious proceedings brought
for purposes other than the assertion of legitimate rights;

(d)
it
is a general characteristic of vexatious proceedings that grounds and issues
raised tend to be rolled forward into subsequent actions and repeated and
supplemented, often with actions brought against the lawyers who have acted for
or against the litigant in earlier proceedings
;

(e) in
determining whether proceedings are vexatious, the court must look at the whole
history of the matter and not just whether there was originally a good cause of
action;

(f) the
failure of the person instituting the proceedings to pay the costs of
unsuccessful proceedings is one factor to be considered in determining whether
proceedings are vexatious;

(g) the
respondent's conduct in persistently taking unsuccessful appeals from judicial
decisions can be considered vexatious conduct of legal proceeding. [Emphasis
added.]

[
101
]

The fourth indicium, that vexatious litigation
has an ‘accumulative’ character, is not specifically reflected in the
Judicature
Act
, s 23(2) list. That is an additional basis on which I could conclude Mr.
Fearn has engaged in vexatious litigation. In

Lee J ordered that the vexatious litigant could only institute legal
proceedings after providing a security for costs deposit.

b.         Costs Awards in
Criminal Proceeding are Exceptional

[
117
]

In a civil (ie. non-criminal matter), costs are
normally awarded in favour of the successful party:
Alberta Rules of Court
,
Alta Reg 124/2010, s 10.29(1) [the “
Rules
” or individually a “
Rule
”].

Meads
does indicate that presumptively a litigant forced to
respond to an OPCA-based court proceeding should be indemnified.

[
118
]

However, I conclude that the application put
before me, no matter its irregularities, is better considered a criminal rather
than civil matter, and in that context very different principles apply. I come
to that conclusion on the basis reviewed by Saunders JA in
R v Taylor
,

2008 NSCA 5
at para
55
, 261 NSR (2d) 247, that the ‘criminal’ presumptions to
costs applies equally to both trial and proceedings associated with a criminal
trial.

[
119
]

In the criminal context an award of costs is an
exceptional, rather than regular occurrence. In
R v 974649 Ontario Inc.
,

2001 SCC 81
, [2001] 3 SCR 575 McLachlin CJC indicates that a cost award against
the Crown is only appropriate in response to an “exceptional or remarkable
event” (at para 85), where Crown conduct is “a marked and unacceptable
departure from the reasonable standards expected of the prosecution.” (at para
87).

[
120
]

The authority to order cost awards in a criminal
law proceeding flows from the inherent jurisdiction of the court (
R v
974649 Ontario Inc.
, at paras
80-81
):

80        ... Costs awards have a long
history as a traditional criminal law remedy. Although sparingly used prior to
the advent of the
Charter
,
superior courts have always possessed the
inherent jurisdiction to award costs against the Crown
: R. v. Ouellette,

1980 CanLII 9 (SCC)
, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 568; R. v. Pawlowski, (1993),
1993 CanLII 3378 (ON CA)
, 12 O.R. (3d) 709 (C.A.), at p.
712 ...

81        Such awards, while not without a
compensatory element,
are integrally connected to the court's control of its
trial process, and intended as a means of disciplining and discouraging
flagrant and unjustified incidents
of non-disclosure. ...

See also
R v Ouellette
,

1980 CanLII 9 (SCC)
, [1980] 1 SCR 568, 111 DLR (3d) 216.

[
121
]

Cost awards against an accused, or his/her counsel,
are even more unusual, and even the possibility of such an award is rarely
addressed. The policy basis for that is explained by Stewart J in
R
v Lebrasseur
(1997),
1997 CanLII 26083 (NS SC)
, 163 NSR (2d) 301, 36 WCB (2d) 21 (NSSC):

... The very scarcity or absence of Canadian
criminal cases is demonstrative of the fact Canadian criminal courts do not
exercise the remedy against defence counsel often, if at all. The concept of
costs would have a chilling effect on the functioning of defence counsel. ...

See also
R v Duarte
,

[2003] OTC 392, 57 WCB (2d) 428 (Ont Sup Ct J)
;
R v Trang
,
2002
ABQB 744
at para
481
, 11 Alta LR (4th) 52.

[
122
]

Put in a
Charter
context, the priority
put by Canadian courts on the right of an accused to make full answer and
defence means that the courts are generous in their evaluation of defence
conduct that has a potentially suspect character.

[
123
]

Nevertheless, courts of inherent jurisdiction clearly
retain a broad authority to order costs in a criminal proceeding. In
Attorney-General
of Quebec et al. v Cronier
(1981),
1981 CanLII 3179 (QC CA)
, 63 CCC (2d) 437 (Que CA), L’Heureux-Dubé
JA (as she then was) described that jurisdiction, at pp 449 and 451:

[TRANSLATION] A superior court has the power
to maintain its authority and to control its procedure so as to put justice in
order and efficiently.
That this implies sometimes ordering one of the
parties and even lawyers to pay the costs of a proceeding in cases of the abuse
or of the frivolity of proceedings, of misconduct or dishonesty or of taken for
some other ulterior motive, is a recognized principle
. But the conditions
for the exercise of this inherent power must exist.

...

In my view, nothing in the present case
authorized the Superior Court Judge to order the appellants to pay costs by
virtue of his inherent powers of control and supervision.

On the one hand, the Judge cannot authorize
himself to do indirectly what the Canadian criminal law does not expressly
authorize him to do, in the present case, the ordering to pay costs with
respect to extraordinary remedies in criminal matters.
In the absence of

d.         Criteria

[

By definition, the arguments employed in each of the surveyed
proceedings were frivolous and vexatious. The schemes used by the accused had
no possibility of success. I believe that employment of OPCA techniques in
these contexts is an abuse of process. In other words, these are incidents that
match the criteria identified by Justice L’Heureux-Dubé in
Attorney-General
of Quebec et al. v Cronier
:

... this implies sometimes ordering one of
the parties and even lawyers to pay the costs of a proceeding
in cases of
the abuse or of the frivolity of proceedings, of misconduct or dishonesty or of
taken for some other ulterior motive
, is a recognized principle. ...

[
132
]

No OPCA technique has ever provided any benefit to an accused
facing criminal charges, other than
illegitimate
benefits and harm to
the public interest including delay, longer and unnecessary hearings, and increased
cost to the court and Crown. In the face of almost two decades of unrelenting,
incessant failure, I impute to OPCA litigants the natural consequence of their
actions: litigation for a dishonest or ulterior motive.

[
133
]

I therefore conclude that, though exceptional, costs may be
awarded against a defendant in a criminal matter who employs OPCA strategies to
cause illegitimate and unnecessary steps in a criminal proceeding. I suggest an
award of that kind may be made where four criteria are met:

1.         the accused is
the one who initiates a hearing, application, or process;

2.         the
accused’s position relies on a clearly illegal or incorrect basis, such as a known,
identified, and rejected OPCA strategy;

3.         the accused is
entirely unsuccessful; and

4.         the
hearing, application, or process is not a direct component of the criminal
trial or sentencing process, but instead is ancillary to the criminal
proceeding itself, for example:

a) a meaningless
application to a different court to challenge the criminal proceeding or court
jurisdiction;

b) an
application to deny trial court jurisdiction;

c) an attempt
to enter irrelevant evidence or witnesses;

d) an application for
representation of the accused by an inappropriate representative, such as an
OPCA guru; and

e) an application for
release of the accused from pre-trial detention outside the judicial interim
release process, such as a frivolous
habeus corpus
application.

[
134
]

It occurs to me that an appeal of a criminal conviction that has
no legitimate basis is another scenario in which a cost award might be
possible, however I believe that question would be better explored in response
to a frivolous appeal or leave to appeal application.

[
135
]

The
Charter
, s 7 right of the accused to make a full
argument and defence is an important reason for why I have restricted these
criteria to award costs for subjects that are separate from the main criminal
trial process itself. It occurs to me that where OPCA concepts emerge in a
trial itself then that misconduct is potentially more relevant as a factor in
sentencing, as occurred in
R v Jastrebske
and
R v Seagull
.
A contempt of court remedy may also be an appropriate response mechanism. My
guidelines on award of costs are therefore intended to contemplate OPCA-based
disruptions in a criminal proceeding that are discrete from the general
criminal trial process.

[
136
]

Returning to the survey of instances where OPCA-based defences
have emerged in a criminal proceeding, I conclude certain reported cases might
be well-suited for a cost award. For example, in
R v Sands
a discrete
court hearing was required in response to an OPCA-based
habeus corpus

application that had no potential for success. The Crown and court committed
resources to an entirely irrelevant and frivolous proceeding.

[
137

Similarly, in
R v Boyer
,
R v Petrie
and
R v Valliere
,
the courts and Crown were forced to respond to pre-trial applications that

b.         Criminal vs Civil
Contempt

[
147
]

Contempt of court exists in two forms: criminal
contempt, and civil contempt. The distinction flows from the degree to which the
contemptuous conduct has a potential
general
effect on the operation of
the court. Criminal contempt is a public activity, while the public exposure
and the resulting influence of misconduct which forms civil contempt is more
limited.

[
148
]

Justice McLachlin (as she then was) in
United
Nurses of Alberta v Alberta (Attorney General)
, at 931-933, identified
the kinds of misconduct that distinguish civil from criminal contempt of court:

... A person who simply breaches a court
order, for example by failing to abide by visiting hours stipulated in a child
custody order, is viewed as having committed civil contempt.
However, when
the element of public defiance of the court's process in a way calculated to
lessen societal respect for the courts is added to the breach, it becomes
criminal
. ...

... The gravamen of the offence is rather
the
open, continuous and flagrant violation of a court order without regard for the
effect that may have on the respect accorded to edicts of the court
.

... To establish criminal contempt the Crown
must prove that the accused defied or disobeyed a court order in a public way
(the actus reus), with intent, knowledge or recklessness as to the fact that
the public disobedience will tend to depreciate the authority of the court (the
mens rea).  The Crown must prove these elements beyond a reasonable doubt.  As
in other criminal offences, however, the necessary mens rea may be inferred
from the circumstances.
An open and public defiance of a court order will
tend to depreciate the authority of the court.  Therefore when it is clear the
accused must have known his or her act of defiance will be public, it may be
inferred that he or she was at least reckless as to whether the authority of
the court would be brought into contempt
. [Emphasis added.]

[
149
]

In
B.C.G.E.U. v British Columbia (Attorney
General)
misconduct that attracts the criminal contempt sanction was
identified by the manner in which it spills outside the in-court dispute and
has a broader effect:

Conduct designed to interfere with the proper
administration of justice constitutes contempt of court which is said to be
"criminal" in that it transcends the limits of any dispute between
particular litigants and constitutes an affront to the administration of
justice as a whole ...

Criminal contempt is therefore also
civil contempt, just with a larger potential area of effect.

[
150
]
