ii.         When Is Speech In
Contempt of Court?

[
163
]

“Behaviour that negligently or recklessly
inevitably results in disrespect for the court can be contemptuous.”:
Royal
Canadian Mounted Police (Re)
,
2008 NWTTC 5
at para
24
, 171 CRR (2d) 86.
Conduct that attacks the social function of the court in providing justice may
also be contempt. In
Koerner v Capital Health Authority
,
2010
ABQB 557
at para
31
, 498 AR 99, Shelley J explained:

... The central idea is that courts have a
right to protect the dignity of their own proceedings, and they are entitled to
discipline any conduct that they feel tarnishes, undermines, or impedes the
court’s role in society as administrator of justice. The Court of Queen’s Bench
has an inherent power to find a person in contempt of court if they feel the
proceedings are being disrespected ...

[
164
]

Do the allegations in Mr. Fearn’s Notice, much
directed exactly at the most basic underpinnings and validity of the Canadian
court system and the judiciary, represent contempt of court? I believe it is
helpful to examine how challenges of this kind have been addressed. Much of the
case law that explores this general question examines criminal contempt, rather
than civil contempt. Court review of conduct that forms criminal contempt is
nevertheless useful, as any misconduct that warrants court response of that
kind would certainly be captured as well as civil contempt.

[
165
]

First, it is clear that the court is generally
cautious and does not rise to defend itself at every critical public or private
expression. For example, in
Alberta (Attorney General) v Edmonton Sun
Publishing Limited
(1981),
1981 CanLII 1097 (AB QB)
, 16 Alta LR (2d) 246, 62 CCC (2d) 318 (Alta
QB) Justice Legg concluded that a cartoon which implied judges were “dirty old
men” did not represent contempt, even though “it is in very bad taste.”

[
166
]

The general rule is found in
Parashuram
Detaram Shamdasani v King-Emperor
,
[1945] AC 264
268-269, endorsed in
R
v Paul; R v Polchies
,
1980 CanLII 37 (SCC)
, [1980] 2 SCR 169, 111 DLR (3d) 626: to be a
contempt, the words tend to bring the administration of justice into disrepute.

[
167
]

The leading post-
Charter
authority on
this subject is
R v Kopyto
(1987),
1987 CanLII 176 (ON CA)
, 62 OR (2d) 449, 47 DLR (4th)
213 (Ont CA), where a five judge panel considered whether a lawyer was in
contempt when he alleged in a media report that a court result was a “mockery
of justice”, “stinks to high hell”, and that the courts did not provide just
results, were a “charade” and “[t]he courts and the RCMP are sticking so close
together you’d think they were put together with Krazy Glue.”: para 7.

[
168
]

R v Kopyto

largely focuses on whether a form of criminal contempt, traditionally called
“scandalizing the court”, is consistent with the free speech rights protected
by
Charter
, s 2(b). Scandalizing the court is speech that is derogatory
or insulting to the court and judiciary. Four separate decisions were written,
with two judges in dissent. I concur with the interpretation of this decision
made by Jeffrey Miller in
The Law of Contempt in Canada
(Scarborough:
Carswell 1997) at p 113 that contempt by speech requires a court find there is
a “clear and present” or “real and imminent” danger that utterances would bring
the administration of justice into disrepute. This is a very high threshold.

[
169
]

Justice Houlden at para
129
indicates the manner
in which a court operates in itself establishes valid social function:

I feel confident that our judiciary and our
courts are strong enough to withstand criticism after a case has been decided
no
matter how outrageous or scurrilous that criticism may be
. I feel equally
confident that the Canadian citizenry are not so gullible that they will lose
faith and confidence in our judicial system because of such criticism.
If
the way in which judges and courts conduct their business commands respect,
then they will receive respect, regardless of any abusive criticism that may be
directed towards them
. ... [Emphasis added.]

[
170
]

Similarly Cory JA (as he then was) observed at
para 33:

... Some criticism may be well founded, some
suggestions for change worth adopting.
But the courts are not fragile
flowers that will wither in the hot heat of controversy
. Rules of evidence,
methods of procedure and means of review and appeal exist that go far to
establishing a fair and equitable rule of law. The courts have functioned well
and effectively in difficult times. They are well-regarded in the community
because they merit respect.
They need not fear criticism nor need they seek
to sustain unnecessary barriers to complaints about their operations or
decisions
. [Emphasis added.]

[
171
]

A similar position has been adopted by other
commentators. Jack Watson (now Watson JA of the Alberta Court of Appeal) in
“Badmouthing the Bench: Is There a Clear and Present Danger? To What?” (1992),
56 Sask L Rev 113 [“
Watson
”] argues any expression of the contempt
authority has a single goal: “protection of justice from ‘clear and present
danger’ to it, i.e. real and imminent harm or threat to justice.” Any potential
for contempt sanction due to ‘scandalizing’ conduct requires “clearly
delineated and discernible boundaries”. He concludes that critical speech
cannot, in itself, be a basis for contempt sanctions given the protected status
of free expression.

[
172
]

There is comparatively little reported case law
that addresses contempt by derogatory or insulting speech. Several cases are
particularly useful. In
R v Cram
(1994),
1994 CanLII 480 (BC SC)
, 95 BCLR (2d) 1, 24 WCB
(2d) 383 (BCSC) the defendant in court and before a large audience alleged
broad corruption in the British Columbia courts, including that judges had
aided and abetted an alleged child molester and defrauded native peoples. A
disbarred lawyer who accompanied the defendant was ejected and the court
adjourned. Cram then encouraged a large group of onlookers to enter the body of
the court. A confrontation with the sheriffs ensued. When the hearing resumed
Cram refused to return to the counsel table and instead insisted on speaking
from the gallery, surrounded by others, his “army”. The presiding judge ordered
Cram arrested.

[
173
]

Cram’s allegations were classified as “wildly
extravagant” and “paranoid”: para 41. Cram’s appearance in court:

... was to turn the court process into a
platform from which to make public allegations which were irrelevant to the
proceedings before the court and to prejudice the rightful interest of the parties
who were there to seek justice from the court.

[
174
]

Cram’s attempt to incite violence from the
observers was clearly contempt (para 42), and the same was true of his refusal
to return to the counsel table (para 43). The court did not decide whether or not
the allegations made in court were or were not criminal contempt, as it appears
no allegation of contempt had been advanced on that basis (para 53).

[
175
]

R v Prefontaine
,
2002 ABQB 980
, 12 Alta LR (4th) 50, also involves in-court
misconduct. Prefontaine, an ex-lawyer, responded negatively on three occasions
when a court decided against him. Each of the three hearings was heard by a
different judge. Prefontaine generally alleged a broad conspiracy involving
judges, lawyers, and the Canada Customs and Revenue Agency. At the contempt
trial evidence was received that Prefontaine had certain psychological
disorders (paras 15-18), and Prefontaine apologied for what he acknowledged was
inappropriate conduct (para 19).

[
176
]

In the first hearing, before the Alberta Court of
Appeal, Prefontaine alleged the judge was a liar, a murderer, and that the
hearing judge was not independent but instead depended on “the thugs at Revenue
Canada and the liars at Justice Canada, your reporting department” (paras
22-24). The judge then terminated the hearing.

[
177
]

The second alleged contempt scenario followed
much the same theme. Again, Prefontaine alleged the judge was biased, not
independent, “pretending to be a judge”, was working for government actors, and
“stand with the liars and thieves and murderers of our society” (paras 28-30).
The matter was adjourned, but after the judge had left the courtroom
Prefontaine stated words to the effect of “If you're going to continue doing
things like that, you'd better get used to living behind bullet proof glass.”
(para 32).

[
178
]

The last hearing where potential contempt
emerged again had Prefontaine argue the hearing judge reported to Revenue
Canada, and that the judge was not independent or unbiased: para 35. When an
unfavourable judgment was issued Prefontaine renewed his allegations and added
the judge was a liar, had not complied with his oath of office, and engaged in
insults and obscenities directed to the court and opposing counsel: paras
35-36.

[
179
]

Moreau J evaluated these three scenarios at
paras 77-80 and concludes that the first and second incidents represent
criminal contempt, not because of the
nature of the language
used, but
because
of its effect
. On those occasions the hearing was terminated as a
consequence of Prefontaine’s outbursts. In the third hearing the judgment was
given and the proceeding effectively complete before Prefontaine began his
tirade.

[
180
]

R v Gillespie
,
2000 MBQB 149
, 149 ManR (2d) 196, affirmed
2000 MBCA 160
, 156 ManR
(2d) 162 evaluates whether certain communications to a judge represent speech
that is criminal contempt. Gillespie telephoned the office of the Chief Justice
of Manitoba and wrote a letter to another judge. Both communications were
highly negative, critical of specific judges, and challenged the judges’ proper
exercise of their roles. That, however, was not a basis to find contempt. What
was relevant were specific threats to the judges in question (paras 30, 36-37):

... In my view, to tell someone that he is
"going to pay" or will be "history" is a threat.

... It is agreed that the Manitoba Warriors
are the most organized and structured street gang in Winnipeg. They have used
intimidation and threats or use of force regularly to dissuade individuals from
reporting matters to the police or to intimidate witnesses or complainants in
court proceedings. A large number of the individuals believed to be active
members and associates have criminal records for violent or weapons related
offences.

I think it can hardly be doubted that to
"fill in" the Manitoba Warriors about anyone would constitute a
threat or an attempt to intimidate.

[
181
]

Justice Morse stresses that the
operational effect

of this communication is immaterial, rather what matters is the communications
were “... acts calculated or intended to interfere with the due administration
of justice ...” and that “... the appearance of interference with the due
administration of justice is sufficient to constitute the offence of contempt
of court.”: paras 8, 11-12.

[
182
]

Last, in
R v High Sierra Broadcasting Ltd.
,

[1990] BCJ No 2982 (QL) (BCSC)
, an individual criticized a number of judges,
including a claim that a particular judge was responsible for the death of a
boy. These criticisms were broadcast several times on a local radio station.
Contempt charges were advanced against the person who made the claims, the
radio station, and a reporter. No contempt was found for the latter two
defendants as neither was aware that the person who advanced the allegations
was at that very time in an action before one of the target judges. However,
the critic not only was a litigant before a target judge, but also on this
basis successfully applied that the target judge recuse himself.

[
183
]

Justice McDonald concluded that result was the
intended effect of the critic’s statements, and as such the accused was in contempt
of court (paras 25-26):

It is indeed unfortunate that Mr.
Boisvert-Gilman was unable to let his strong, and I believe genuine, feelings
about Judge Arkell, be known in a more conventional way. ... Mr.
Boisvert-Gilman has the capacity to disregard facts and to accept unfounded
allegations whenever and wherever it suits his convenience or fits his
particular thesis. He has no comprehension or concern for the judicial process
itself or those who are charged with its administration. While the latter may
not be a concern in light of the development of the law of contempt, as
exemplified in Regina vs. Kopyto and its application of the freedom of speech
provisions of the
Charter
,
the effect of his allegations, generally unfair
and unfounded as they are, on the progress of the Court's business has already
been felt
. [Emphasis added.]

[
184
]

A common theme emerges from these cases: the
substance of language is of less relevance
than its effect or intended
effect
. The relevant jurisprudence is uniform. Contempt can flow from
obnoxious, insulting, or derogatory comments, but only when that communication
consequentially
disrupts the court process itself
. In
R v Cram

the contemptuous speech led to adjournments and in-court disorder. Similarly,
the convictions in
R v Prefontaine
were only where Prefontaine’s
verbal attacks disrupted the court proceeding itself. The findings of criminal
contempt in
R v Gillespie
relate to an attempt to manipulate the
operation of the court via threats. The scandalous comments in
R v High
Sierra Broadcasting Ltd.
were a contempt of court because they led to a
hearing being terminated when a judge recused himself on that basis.

iii.        Legal Effect of the
Notice

[
185
]

The January 13, 2014 hearing was unremarkable in
that sense. Mr. Fearn conducted himself in an appropriate manner, and the court
was able to reach a decision.

[
186
]

The Notice as a whole, which is consistent with
Mr. Fearn’s in-court submissions, is clearly calculated and intended to attack
the essential validity of the Canadian court apparatus, the role of the
judiciary as an independent, impartial arbiter of justice, and the rule of law
itself. There is no need to parse Mr. Fearn’s position. It is self-evident.

[
187
]

Even though Mr. Fearn’s statements are
extraordinary, those ‘insulting’ statements cannot in themselves form a basis
for a finding of contempt. This seems counterintuitive, as Mr. Fearn’s conduct
is the very definition of hostile and insulting, and he directly challenges the
independence and fair operation of the court. He openly declares himself in
contempt of the court process and its actors. How could this not be contemptuous?

[
188
]

While Mr. Fearn’s written materials are wildly
obnoxious, those written submissions were only peripheral to the hearing
process and as a consequence, even though the Notice is both absurd and
troubling, that document itself and its contents did not disrupt or impede the application
process and court hearing. He was respectful to me in Court.

[
189
]

I stress that had speech of this kind occurred
in the hearing then that would have led to directions from the bench that, if
ignored, may result in sanction. All court participants, including Mr. Fearn,
are obliged to follow court instruction.

[
190
]

That said, a further exploration of the
interrelationship of contempt and the OPCA phenomena is appropriate. My conclusion
that contempt is intended to protect against ‘active disruption’ to the
operation of the court system and access to justice raises a further range of OPCA-related
scenarios in which contempt occurs. This is also directly relevant to Mr.
Fearn’s submissions, as he employs some of these potentially contemptuous
techniques.

e.         Attack on Court
Processes and Authority

[
191
]

I conclude OPCA schemes by their very nature may
be a basis for a finding of civil contempt. I again stress the contempt
authority is a
functional
tool to protect court operations:

B.C.G.E.U.
v British Columbia (Attorney General)
,
1988 CanLII 3 (SCC)
, [1988] 2
SCR 214 at 234, 53 DLR (4th) 1:

In some instances the phrase "contempt
of court" may be thought to be unfortunate because, as in the present
case, it does not posit any particular aversion, abhorrence or disdain of the
judicial system. In a legal context the phrase is much broader than the common
meaning of "contempt" might suggest and embraces "where a
person, whether a party to a proceeding or not,
does any act which may tend
to hinder the course of justice or show disrespect to the court's
authority", "interfering with the business of the court on the part
of a person who has no right to do so", "obstructing or attempting to
obstruct the officers of the Court on their way to their duties
" ...

R v
Cohn
(1984),
1984 CanLII 43 (ON CA)
, 15 CCC (3d) 150 at 156, 13 DLR (4th)
680 (Ont CA):

... Conduct which amounts to contempt
outside the court may be described in general terms as words spoken or
otherwise published, or acts done, outside court
which are intended or
likely to interfere with or obstruct the fair administration of justice
.
...

Attorney-General
v Leveller Magazine Ltd.
,
[1979] AC 440 at p 449,
[1979] 1 All ER 745 (HL)
:

... although criminal contempt of court may
take a variety of forms they all share a common characteristic:
they involve
an interference with the due administration of justice
either in a
particular case or more generally as a continuing process.

[Emphasis added.]

[
192
]

R v Gillespie
makes clear that a threat to the operation of a court, even a threat
that has no real prospect to influence the course of justice, may be
contemptuous:
R v Gillespie
, at para 11. In
R v Froese

(1980),
1980 CanLII 428 (BC CA)
, 23 BCLR 181, 54 CCC (2d) 315 (BCCA), Nemetz CJBC explained:

... the test to be applied in cases of this
kind: whether the words spoken and broadcast were calculated to interfere with
the course of justice. In order to make a finding of guilt, it is not necessary
to find either that the words were intended to interfere, or that they did in
fact interfere with the course of justice - for it will often be impossible to
discover the effect of any statement upon a jury.
It is only necessary to be
satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that the words were calculated to interfere

in the sense of being apt, or having a tendency, to do so ... [Emphasis added.]

[
193
]

Similarly, C.J. Miller,
Contempt of Court
(Oxford:
Clarendon Press, 1999) [“
Miller
”], states at p 162-163:

... an intention improperly to interfere
with the due administration of justice will constitute a contempt
even
though it may be safely assumed from the outset that the defendant has
absolutely no chance of succeeding
. ... [Emphasis added.]

[
194
]

A variety of well-characterized OPCA strategies
have emerged that are obviously intended to either disrupt court operations or
intimidate the judiciary. Many of these categories are generally reviewed in
Meads
.
Mr. Fearn’s materials includes several examples. It is easy to conclude that a
person who employs these strategies and directs them against the court is in civil
contempt of court, because each of these scenarios is intended to interfere
with the proper exercise of court authority and court operation. None should be
tolerated; all are ineffective and a waste of expensive and limited resources.
These schemes also distort and mischaracterize the relationship of the
judiciary and public in a manner that interferes with court function.

i.          Foisted Unilateral
Agreements

[
195
]

A common but mistaken OPCA belief is that a
person may make a demand that the recipient of a document rebut certain claims
within a timeline; failure to do so means the recipient has admitted the truth
of those statements, or accepted certain outcomes. Mr. Fearn’s “estoppel”
notices are examples of this scheme. In
Meads
this general
category are identified as “foisted unilateral agreements”: paras 447-528.
Naturally these have no legal effect:
Meads
, at paras
458-472
.
While documents of this kind are often directed to opposing litigants, they also
sometimes target the court itself:
Meads
, at para
480
. A common
variation on this form is that an OPCA litigant unilaterally foists fiduciary
status on a judge:
Meads
himself, at para
11, 22, 39-40, 493
;
Bank
of Montreal v McCance
,
2012 ABQB 537
at para
6
. In other cases a
foisted unilateral contract allegedly negates the authority of the court:
R
v Jastrebske
, at paras
8-9
.

[
196
]

An attempt by an OPCA litigant to use this
procedure to restrict or stop court operations is an illegal attempt to
interfere with the administration of justice.
It is wrong
. If a litigant
directs a document of this kind to the court and then argues the judge is
restricted on that basis, that incorrect/illegal step would not only be
ineffective, it is a challenge to the operation of the court which I conclude would
be
prima facie
civil contempt.

ii.         Fee Schedules

[
197
]

Fee schedules are a common subtype of the
foisted unilateral agreement category:
Meads
, at paras
505-523
.
These documents purport that the recipient is deemed to agree to pay certain
amounts if an event occurs. For example, an OPCA litigant may advance a fee
schedule  which states that a judge must pay the litigant a certain amount if
the litigant is obliged to testify, for ordering a litigant detained, or for
finding against an OPCA litigant. Canadian jurisprudence reports attempts by
OPCA litigants to apply fee schedules against the judiciary:
Meads
,
para
519
;
Canada v Rudolf
,
2010 BCSC 565
at paras
7-9
;
Services
de financement TD inc. c Michaud
,
2011 QCCQ 14868
at para
9
;
Bank of Montreal v McCance
, at para
24
.

[
198
]

The alarming scenario described in
R v
Leis
,
2008 SKQB 123
, 77 WCB (2d) 323 and
R v Leis
,
2008
SKCA 93
illustrates how fee schedules that target a member of the judiciary can
have ongoing, and escalating effects. Leis appeared at the residence of the
judge who had sentenced Leis to a period of incarceration, and then demanded
payment of over $2 million in “fees” and “damages”. This was accompanied by
invoices and newspaper articles to that effect. Leis was convicted of intimidating
a justice system participant (
Criminal Code
, s 423.1) and received an 18
month conditional sentence, which he subsequently breached with yet more
foisted unilateral agreements.

[
199
]

Fee schedules are identified in
Meads

as a tool of intimidation and a potential basis for charges under the
Criminal
Code
. Associate Chief Justice Rooke suggested in
Meads
that
an attempt to apply a fee schedule against a justice system participant is
prima
facie
evidence of intimidation of a justice system participant:
Criminal
Code
, s. 423.1. I agree, and further conclude that any claim to assert a
fee schedule against a hearing judge would be civil contempt of court that warrants
judicial response.

[
200
]

Mr. Fearn’s Notice attaches several documents
that are fee schedules. In particular, his Exhibit 4, “Solemn Asseveration of
Criminal Complaint” includes two documents entitled “Notice and Demand” to
Langston J and Fraser, CJA. These include fee schedule based threats. If these
were directed to this Court and myself I would conclude Mr. Fearn was in
contempt of court.

iii.        Threats of
Extrajudicial Prosecution or Sanction

[
201
]

Another extremely disquieting aspect of certain
OPCA movements is a belief that individuals are authorized to take
extrajudicial vigilante actions against court actors, including judges.
Naturally, these illegal actions are cloaked with some kind of purported though
fictitious authority, most commonly as an expression of the “mutant” common law
in a jury or court process. Typical language is formation of “common law”,
“people’s” or “
de jure
” posses, juries, and trials. Other times OPCA
litigants announce they are forming their own court, on the spot, using their “personal
inherent jurisdiction”. A third related scenario is where an OPCA litigant
claims that it is
notaries
who are the true judges or possess some
supervisory, judicial authority:
Meads
, at paras
273-275
. An
example of this occurred in
Jabez Financial Services Inc. (Receiver of) v
Sponagle
,
2008 NSSC 112
at paras
14
, 264 NSR (2d) 224 where the
defendant claimed:

Whereas it is my understanding that I can
use a Notary Public to perform duties found under any Act including thus they
have the power to hold court and hear evidence and issue binding lawful
judgments, and,

Whereas it is my understanding that a Notary
Public can also be used to bring criminal charges to bear against traitors,
even if they hold the highest office ...

[
202
]

Othertimes OPCA litigants will threaten judges
with sanctions from international courts and tribunals, real or imaginary.

[
203
]

Fortunately, to date this kind of claim appears
unusual in Canada and other commonwealth countries. One example is from
Australia, where in
Hedley v Spivey
, [2012] WASCA 116 at para 19 the
OPCA litigant claimed that the appeal panel would be subject to criminal
charges from a “jura court”:

... are you a jura court and you have
already agreed with a tacit agreement that you are a corporation sitting here
masquerading as judges. Now, I've informed you of that and that carries serious
penalties, ma'am. Once we form a jura court you will be facing criminal
charges. ...

[
204
]

Meads
at
para
124
reports that Freeman-on-the-Land guru Robert Arthur Menard operates a group
of self-declared and appointed vigilante “peace officers”, the “Canadian Common
Corps Of Peace Officers” (“C3PO”).

[
205
]

Reference and reliance on the authority of these
fictitious, vigilante courts and law enforcement officers is a much more common
theme in the US Sovereign Citizen/Man movement. Stephen A. Kent & Robin D.
Willey, “Sects, Cults, and the Attack on Jurisprudence” (2013) 14 Rutgers’
Journal of Law & Religion 306 at 319-329 provides a useful but very
troubling review of that phenomenon and how members of the Sovereign
Citizen/Men movement members use these techniques to challenge and subvert
court and state authority. In that jurisdiction these vigilante processes have
been associated with attempts to abduct, try, and kill judges. A recent Alberta
case involved a Montana Freeman who had participated in this kind of scheme in
the US:
Perreal v Knibb
,
2014 ABQB 15
.

[
206
]

An OPCA litigant who states a judge is potentially
or actually subject to extralegal retaliation or supervision is
prima facie

in contempt of court. Persons who appear in Canadian courts have
well-established avenues to protect their legal rights, including the right of
appeal to the appropriate court and judicial review.

[
207
]

Mr. Fearn’s materials include examples of these
kind of contemptuous claims. In the Exhibit 4, “Solemn Asseveration of Criminal
Complaint”, he at paras 103-105 orders the arrest and trial of three judges for
various offences, including treason, obstruction of justice, and murder. A later
“Statement” claims the right:

... to arrest anyone who make unlawful legal
determinations for Me ... as an
Unprovoked Assault
upon My rights
... with the amount of force that is necessary. [sic, emphasis in original].

He also claims the right to seize
and sell their assets.

[
208
]

However, most alarming is language that appears
in a number of documents attached to the Notice, where Mr. Fearn makes
statements directed to members of the judiciary such as:

... I am not going to rest until I see each of
them
do that little dance they do at the end of a common law rope
,
because they are their ringleaders, amongst other things, in the international
criminal corporation called Canada,
and I will do it all within the law

... [Emphasis added.]

I think it is fair to conclude that
Mr. Fearn here is referring to ‘his law’, rather than Canadian law.

[
209
]

Again, these statements were not directed
specifically to me or to this proceeding. However, if they were, these would
form
prima facie
evidence of contempt of court and warrant sanction:
R
v Gillespie
.

[
210
]

It occurs to me that if a fee schedule is
prima
facie
evidence of the act and intention to intimidate a justice system
participant (
Criminal Code
, s. 423.1) (
Meads
, para
527
,
this decision para 198) then speech of this kind that threatens extrajudicial
response directed to a judge or court personnel may also qualify as a
foundation for that offence.

iv.        Liens and other
Registered Claims

[
211
]

A fourth category of action that represents
contempt of court is the use of or threat to use property or financial
registrations against a judge in response to judicial action. This most
commonly takes the form of liens registered against a judge’s property:
Meads
,
paras
175, 181, 482
;
Canada v Rudolf
,
2010 BCSC 565
at para
8
.
Other variations on this kind of attack include false Personal Property
Registry and Uniform Commercial Code claims:
Squamish Indian Band
v Capilano Mobile Park
,
2011 BCSC 470
paras
66-68
, affirmed
2012 BCCA
126
, 318 BCAC 239. In that case foisted unilateral agreements were the
pseudolegal basis for the subsequent illegal registered claims. Again, any indication
by a litigant that they will respond to court action by taking these steps is
civil contempt of court.

v.         Conclusion - Attack on
Court Processes and Authority

[
212
]

The four OPCA strategies I have identified which
directly attack court operation and therefore are civil contempt of court are
only examples. This is not an exclusive list; other variations may arise. I
stress this analysis should in no way be seen to restrict the right of persons
to challenge judicial authority and conduct by legitimate mechanisms such as
appeal, judicial review, and so on. Those are critical rights available to each
person in Canada.

[
213
]

However, this Court will not tolerate threats of
illegal or vigilante action directed at the judiciary and court staff. Where
those acts then also disrupt court operation then they may also represent
criminal contempt.

[
214
]

Mr. Fearn’s materials include these prohibited,
contemptuous motifs. Nevertheless, I do not believe he specifically challenged
my authority or interfered with my conduct of the Jan. 13, 2014 hearing. I
therefore do not have a basis to find him in civil contempt of court.

f.          Guru Activities as
Criminal Contempt

[
215
]

My conclusion that certain OPCA arguments are
inherently contemptuous when directed at the judiciary and court process leads
to a further issue that involves a unique aspect of the OPCA phenomenon. The
beliefs expressed by persons affiliated with these communities, and the
techniques employed by OPCA affiliates, are often together promoted as a
commercial product. Put simply, there are people whose business is to teach
others methods to circumvent court authority. They promise their customers little
known mechanisms that they claim can frustrate, immobilize, or ‘break’ the
courts. Those secrets are available, but at a price.

[
216
]

As I have previously indicated, this ‘source’
for OPCA concepts is a potentially valid subject for this Court’s comment,
particularly in light of the extreme form in which Mr. Fearn expresses his
variation on the Sovereign Citizen/Man approach, and how he and his peers
direct themselves to the state and judicial apparatus.

i.          The OPCA Guru

[
217
]

In
Meads
the OPCA community is
described as a two tier structure:

•

persons who sell instructional material and
training in OPCA schemes: called “gurus” (paras 85-158);

•

the gurus’ luckless customers (paras 159-167).

[
218
]

That judgment identifies certain OPCA gurus by
name, and details aspects of the schemes they promote. It also explains that
gurus may in certain instances directly participate in litigation by their
customers (para 156) (this was particularly the case for Detaxer guru David
Kevin Lindsay (para 104)). However, often a guru is hidden in the background,
providing advice and materials (para 154-155), but invisible to the court.

[
219
]

OPCA gurus are the ‘Typhoid Marys’ of the OPCA
phenomenon. Rooke ACJ in
Meads
states at para
72
:

The persons who advance these schemes, and
particularly those who market and sell these concepts as commercial products,
are parasites that must be stopped.

I entirely agree.

[
220
]

In
Meads
, Rooke ACJ instructs an
OPCA guru should never be permitted to represent a litigant in court: 614-618.
I agree, but add that direct participation by a guru in court may be a basis
for a finding of civil contempt, following my analysis above.

[
221
]

It occurs to me that the Court’s contempt
authority is an appropriate vehicle to address certain OPCA guru activities
because they are, simply put, at attack on the court and its function.

ii.         Criminal Contempt Directed to Third-Persons to
Litigation

[
222
]

Contempt of court is usually exercised in
response to misconduct that occurs in a courtroom or court proceeding. However,
that is not the only way the contempt authority screens court operations.

[
223
]

I have previously surveyed how case law that
evaluates derogatory speech directed to the courts only represents criminal
contempt when that speech has a deleterious effect, or is intended to have a
deleterious effect:
R v Cram
;
R v Prefontaine
;
R
v Gillespie
;
R v High Sierra Broadcasting Ltd.

[
224
]

Public statements by persons uninvolved in
litigation may trigger a finding of contempt. For example, the “
contempt sub
judice
” concept permits court response where a person publishes information
that may affect a court proceeding, such as causing prejudice to an accused:
Alberta
v The Edmonton Sun
,
2003 ABCA 3
, 221 DLR (4th) 438;
Alberta (AG)
v Interwest Publications Ltd
(1990),
1990 CanLII 2620 (AB QB)
, 73 DLR (4th) 83, 108 AR 173 (Alta
QB);
R v Bowes Publishers Ltd.

(1995), 171 AR 55, 30 Alta LR (3d)
236 (Alta QB)
. What is required is that “... the publication constitutes a real
and substantial risk of prejudice to the administration of justice ...”:
Alberta
v The Edmonton Sun
, at para
63
.

[
225
]

United Nurses of Alberta v Alberta
(Attorney General)
provides another context
where the contempt of court authority has a broader application. In that
decision the majority confirmed that statements made by a union that defied a
court order were criminal contempt. However, once more that is linked to the
effect

of defying a court order (para 55):

To establish criminal contempt the Crown
must prove that the accused defied or disobeyed a court order in a public way
(the actus reus),
with intent, knowledge or recklessness as to the fact that
the public disobedience will tend to depreciate the authority of the court (the
mens rea)
. The Crown must prove these elements beyond a reasonable doubt.
As in other criminal offences, however, the necessary mens rea may be inferred
from the circumstances. An open and public defiance of a court order
will
tend to depreciate the authority of the court
. ... [Emphasis added.]

[
226
]

Lord Diplock in
A.-G. v Leveller Magazine
Ltd.
,
[1979] AC 440 at p 449, [1979] 1 All ER 745 (HL)
also stressed
that contemptuous behaviour is evaluated on its effect:

... they all share a common characteristic:
they involve an interference with the due administration of justice either in a
particular case
or more generally as a continuing process
. [Emphasis
added.]

[
227
]

I therefore conclude that the contempt authority,
as an aspect of the inherent jurisdiction of the superior courts, can potentially
extend to sanction conduct by persons who are not directly before the court or
involved in litigation, provided those persons engage in conduct that
interferes with court processes and authority. That would include the quite
unprecedented phenomenon of individuals who instruct others to apply techniques
that ‘break’ or ‘disrupt’ court function.

iii.        Criminal Contempt may Result from Communication to a
Specific Target Group

[
228
]

In
R v Kopyto
, the Ontario Court
of Appeal frames communications that cause criminal contempt via what effect a
contemptuous communication has on the public
as a whole
. On that basis
the court concludes that a frankly absurd allegation or instruction is unlikely
to affect the perception of the public, and therefore the proper administration
of justice.

[
229
]

It is quite clear that OPCA gurus speak to only
a small proportion of the Canadian population. Most Canadians, for example,
would simply by amused by the proposition that a court’s function may be
affected by the existence or absence of a gold thread fringe on a flag in a
courtroom:
Meads
, at para
272
;
R v JBC Securities Ltd.
,

2003 NBCA 53
at paras
2
, 9, 261 N.B.R. (2d) 199. However, it is unnecessary
that this kind of speech by gurus affect the perceptions of the general public.

[
230
]

I think a distinction should exist between
speech that potentially attacks the function of the court as a whole by
subverting its public authority, and a very distinct and different scenario, what
is essentially training for “paper terrorism” then conducted by a limited
number of litigants and potential litigants. The function of the contempt
authority is clear: alleged contempt degrades or is intended to degrade the
operation of the court apparatus. In that sense OPCA techniques have a direct
effect, even when implemented by a small proportion of the overall Canadian
population. Simply put, it does not take too many misguided but energetic
persons to ‘gum up’ court function.

[
231
]

In a sense times have changed since
R v
Kopyto
. OPCA concepts, a new pathogenic and inveigled meme that few in
the public or judiciary likely could have imagined but a few years ago, has spread
from the United States into Canada. Though insubstantial, this cloud of
concepts nevertheless provides, at least for some, a basis to hold a sadly
ungrounded belief that state and court authority is illegitimate. Those who
subscribe to and apply these ideas, such as Mr. Fearn, argue strange,
disjointed, alternative histories drenched in conspiracy and malice. These
people are not benign co-travellers in our nation. They misuse legal processes,
and claim extraordinary authority, as reviewed by Kent, above.

[
232
]

In particular, Mr. Fearn belongs to a group that
is notoriously for their violent conduct, intimidation of state and court
personnel, and “paper terrorism”:
Meads
, at para
181
; Robert
Chamberlain & Donald P. Haider-Markel, “"Lien on Me": State
Policy Innovation in Response to Paper Terrorism” (2005) 58 Polit Research
Quart 449; Erick J. Haynie, “Populism, Free Speech, and the Rule of Law: The
"Fully Informed" Jury Movement and Its Implications” (1997) 88 J Crim
L & Criminology 343; Susan P. Koniak “When Law Risks Madness” (1996) 8
Cardozo Stud L & Literature 65; Wilson Huhn, “Political Alienation in
America and The Legal Premises of the Patriot Movement” (1999) 34 Gonz L Rev
417; Michelle Theret, “Sovereign Citizens: A Homegrown Terrorist Threat and its
Negative Impact on South Carolina” (2012) 63 S C L Rev 853; Francis X. Sullivan,
“The "Usurping Octopus of Jurisdictional/Authority": The Legal
Theories of the Sovereign Citizen Movement” (1999) Wis L Rev 785. The
seriousness of this threat is indicated by the fact the FBI classifies
Sovereign Citizens/Men as a domestic terrorist movement.

[
233
]

Though it might be a comfort to imagine this kind
of belief is the product of a disordered mind, forensic psychology
investigation of persons who espouse these beliefs and their legal capacity in
court have instead concluded these are honest political opinions, reinforced by
participation in marginal subcommunities: Jennifer Pytyck and Gary A.
Chaimowitz, “The Sovereign Citizen Movement and Fitness to Stand Trial” (2013)
International Journal of Forensic Mental Health, 12:2, p 149-153. The depth to
which these ideas are held is disturbing. For example, Dale Jacobi, a Montana
Freemen, recently appeared in this Court asserting OPCA concepts, even though
he had only just completed an over 13 year prison sentence in the United
States:
Perreal v Knibb
.

[
234
]

I therefore conclude that criminal contempt does
not merely result from speech that tends to bring the administration of
justice, as perceived by the public as a whole, into disrepute. What is
necessary is that the communication causes “a real and substantial risk of
prejudice to the administration of justice”, which may occur directly or via
intermediaries.

iv.        Why OPCA Gurus are Potential Subjects for Criminal
Contempt Proceedings

[
235
]

The courts are consistent that the contempt
authority is to be used sparingly, where conduct causes a “serious public
injury”: reviewed in
R v Glasner
(1994),
1994 CanLII 3444 (ON CA)
, 19 OR (3d) 739, 119 DLR
(4th) 113 (Ont CA). I conclude the activities of OPCA gurus may, in certain
instances, meet that threshold.

(a)        OPCA Schemes Impede
Court Function

[
236
]

Justice Saunders of the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal in two recent
cases commented on how wasteful, vexatious litigation has become an intolerable
and unacceptable burden on the courts. One of the two litigants was a ‘garden
variety’ vexatious litigant who had initiated at least 103 lawsuits (
Doncaster
v Chignecto-Central Regional School Board
,
2013 NSCA 59
, 330 NSR (2d)
82), while the other applied as assortment of OPCA strategies (
MacDonald
v First National Financial GP Corp.
,
2013 NSCA 60
, 330 NSR (2d) 115). Saunders
JA decisively rejects these approaches. They are nothing less than an attack on
the court apparatus itself:

[46] Litigants, self-represented or not,
with a different
agenda designed to wreak havoc on the system by a succession of endless,
mindless or mind-numbing paper or electronic filings, or meant to drive a
spouse or opposite party to distraction or despair or financial ruin
will
quickly come to realize that the Court's patience, tolerance and largesse have
worn thin.
They and their cases will be seen as an affront to justice and
summarily shown the door
.

[47] More often than not, the individuals in this latter
group whom I would dub "self-serving litigants" leave a trail of
unpaid judgments and costs orders in their wake.
Judges will not sit idly by
as the finite resources of their courts are hijacked by people with computer
skills or unlimited time on their hands; at the expense of worthy matters,
waiting patiently in the queue for a hearing. Faux litigants will be exposed,
soon earning the tag "vexatious litigant" or "paper
terrorist" whose offerings deserve a sharp rebuff and rebuke
.

[48] Over the past two months I have encountered several such
cases. Their number is mounting. I find that troubling. The Bench, the
practicing Bar and the public should be concerned.
This trespass upon
legitimate advocacy is not in the public interest. In the short term it
frustrates the efficient passage and completion of litigation. In the long term
it erodes and denigrates confidence in and respect for the administration of
justice. It defeats a system of dispute resolution managed and overseen by
people who are doing the best they can to serve the public in a way that
respects and follows the law, and produces a result that satisfies the primary
object of the Rules which is to provide "for the just, speedy and
inexpensive determination of every proceeding"
. [Emphasis added.]

Justice Saunders’ comments were subsequently
endorsed by the Quebec Court of Appeal:
Mazhero v CBC/Radio-Canada
,

2014 QCCA 107
at paras
43-44
, JE 2014-215.

[
237
]

I agree with Justice Saunders that misuse of court resources and
processes by vexatious litigants, including OPCA litigants, represents a
genuine threat to the function and operation of court processes. Canadian
jurisprudence provides ample examples of how the techniques
taught by OPCA gurus frustrate and complicate court proceedings.

[
238
]

I have previously reviewed examples of those in
my discussion of how certain OPCA strategies are
prima facie
civil
contempt of court. My review of criminal proceedings where OPCA concepts have
been deployed also illustrates how the purported remedies taught by OPCA gurus
complicate court proceedings in a needless, useless manner. In fact, these
strategies make things worse. For example, in
R v Jastrebske
,
and
R v Seagull
the offenders received a
stricter
sentence
because they had disobeyed court authority in their attempts to apply OPCA
strategies.

[
239
]

The
Meads
judgment provides many
additional examples of how OPCA concepts impede court function:

•

futile attempts to defeat court authority via
arguments that a court is somehow defective (paras 286-297), or has a limited
jurisdiction (paras 302-340);

•

instructions that individuals before the court
must engage in bizarre, disruptive behaviour to avoid entering into an
imaginary contract with the court (paras 414-416); and

•

litigants engaging in a “song and dance” where
they are somehow split into two halves, both of which may, in some manner, be
involved in a court proceeding (paras 440-446).

[
240
]

All of these things waste court time, increase
the duration and cost of litigation, and provide absolutely no benefit to those
OPCA litigants who attempt to employ them. Instead, they face elevated or indemnity
costs (
Meads
, at paras
596
. 631;
A.N.B. v Hancock
,
at para
97-100
), vexatious litigant status (
Meads
, at para
613
;
Yankson
v Canada (Attorney General)
,
2013 BCSC 2332
)), and potential contempt
of court sanctions (this decision, above at paras 191-214).

[
241
]

The reported case law only hints at the
additional grief caused when litigants attempt to apply these strategies, often
in response to extreme stress: Stephen A. Kent, “Freemen, Sovereign Citizens,
and the Threat to Public Order in British Heritage Countries”, paper delivered
at the European Federation of Centres of Research and Information on
Sectarianism (FECRIS), Copenhagen, Denmark (May 30, 2013). In
Meads
,
at para
161
, Rooke ACJ identifies a range of examples where it appears
individuals in extreme distress have adopted these futile strategies, for
example during a home foreclosure, a bankruptcy, or to avoid deportation.
Subsequent to that decision the courts have reported more of the same:

•

foreclosure:
First National Financial GP
Corporation v Maritime Residential Housing Development Ltd.
,
2013 NSSC
219
;
Scotia Mortgage Corporation v Gutierrez
,
2012 ABQB 683
;
1158997
Alberta Inc v Maple Trust Company
,
2013 ABQB 483
; and

•

children being seized by their parents:
A.N.B.
v Alberta (Minister of Human Services)
;
A.R. v Alberta (Child,
Youth and Family Enhancement Act Director)
,
2013 ABQB 280
;
J.A. v
New Brunswick (Minister of Social Development),

2013 NBQB 137
.

This only hints at the misery
aggravated by the concepts sold by OPCA gurus. Trial judges in this
jurisdiction regularly encounter desperate persons who squander their remaining
limited resources on futile OPCA responses.

[
242
]

Even in the face of an active, informed court,
OPCA concepts continue to unnecessarily cause expenditure of limited court
resources, and contribute to the well documented access to justice issue, as
described in
Hryniak v Mauldin
,
2014 SCC 7
. I therefore conclude
this interference with court function and access to justice is a “clear and
present danger”, and “real and imminent harm or threat to justice”:
Miller

at p 113;
Watson
at p 136.

(b)       Criminal
Contempt Prosecution of OPCA Gurus Responds to Attack on Court Function

[
243
]

To be explicit, not all OPCA concepts are
directed towards the court and its procedures. Certain other ideas promoted by OPCA
gurus are therefore
not
a potential basis for a charge or conviction for
criminal contempt of court.

[
244
]

For example, teaching OPCA concepts that
purportedly defeat income tax obligation is counselling fraud:
Criminal Code
,
ss 380(1)(a), 464, see
R v Porisky
;
R v Joseph Blerot
,

2014 SKQB 2
. Presumably an OPCA guru who advances a “money for nothing” scheme
such as “A4V” (
Meads
, at paras
531-543
) could also be the subject
of a criminal prosecution for counselling fraud.  The laws of Parliament cover
this.

[
245
]

OPCA gurus often argue a very commonplace but
misguided belief that legal operation of a motor vehicle does not require a
driver’s licence or motor vehicle insurance: for example,
R v Furqan
,

2013 NSCA 55
;
R v Westover
,
2013 ONCJ 472
;
R v Valliere
,

2013 ONCJ 158
.

[
246
]

Promoting this concept also does not represent a
basis for a contempt sanction; that challenge is to
a law
, not
the
authority of the courts
. Some alternative sanction, perhaps counselling
mischief, may instead be an appropriate response.

(c)        OPCA
Gurus a Special Category of Suitable Criminal Contempt Targets

[
247
]

Canadian jurisprudence reviewed above is clear
that the court’s contempt authority is an unusual process, used in a sparing
and cautious manner. That is particularly true when the alleged contempt occurs
outside the court. That said, OPCA gurus themselves are an unusual, if not
unprecedented, category. These individuals are therefore appropriate
exceptional targets, because:

1.         The ideas promoted by these individuals harm their
customers, other innocent litigants, the state, and the court.

2.         OPCA gurus are often behind the scenes, and largely
‘invisible’ to the court itself. We only see their downstream effects. They are
therefore unlikely to become targets of civil contempt sanction.

3.         Almost two decades of in-court failure has neither
deterred these promoters nor their customers. Rooke ACJ explains this is at
least in part due to the gurus attributing failure to misuse by their customers
of the techniques taught (para 78), that OPCA gurus themselves often do not use
the techniques they teach (though they say they do) (paras 668, 674-675), and
the manner in which OPCA schemes are taught in an unnecessarily byzantine,
ornamented, and magical manner (paras 77, 80). A more direct challenge is
therefore an appropriate strategy.

4.         OPCA gurus are uniquely obnoxious in that they not only
make victims of the court and their own customers, but they do so in a
commercial
context
,
for profit
, operating a cottage industry of seminars,
training materials, and tutorials. OPCA gurus engage in
a business
that
causes real social and individual harm. They are a malevolent, dark mirror
reflection of the legal profession.

5.         OPCA gurus engage in activity that parallels the
components of criminal counselling offences, as described in
R v Hamilton
,

2005 SCC 47
, [2005] 2 SCR 432:

a) “... the

actus reus
for counselling will be established where the materials or
statements made or transmitted by the accused actively induce or advocate — and
do not merely describe — the commission of an offence” (para 15);

b) “... the

mens rea
consists in nothing less than an accompanying intent or
conscious disregard of the substantial and unjustified risk inherent in the
counselling: that is, it must be shown that the accused either intended that
the offence counselled be committed, or knowingly counselled the commission of
the offence while aware of the unjustified risk that the offence counselled was
in fact likely to be committed as a result of the accused’s conduct.” (para.
29);

6.         To date OPCA gurus have had no reason to change or
terminate their activities. Their misconduct has had no consequences. Instead,
the damage they cause has been implicitly tolerated. It is time for that to
end.

[
248
]

In brief, to date there has been a lacuna in the
court and state response to OPCA litigation. Many OPCA gurus appear to operate
unchecked, particularly as their ‘victim’ is an entity, the court, which is
very cautious about the exercise of its powers in a public context. That said,
criminal contempt is a potential remedy for that injured party to address abuse
of its processes. There is no legislation that specifically responds to this
form of misconduct, so I conclude suppression of OPCA guru activities is a
context where the common law contempt authority may potentially be applied to
protect court operation via prosecutions for criminal contempt of court.

(d)       A Threshold For Court Response, and Punitive
Steps

[
249
]

Commercial promotion of OPCA concepts directly
intended to frustrate and impede court processes is a potential basis for a
criminal contempt of court prosecution.

[
250
]

A more detailed exploration of what range and
kind of factors would be relevant to evaluate that misconduct, for example to
determine an appropriate sanction or what kind or scale of activity would meet
the threshold of a “real and substantial risk of prejudice to the
administration of justice”, is better developed in the context of a specific
fact scenario.

[
251
]

What is, however, clear from the jurisprudence
that I have reviewed is that a critical factor will be the
intention
to
disrupt, whether unsuccessful or not:
R v Gillespie
;
R v
Froese
.

[
252
]

It also occurs to me that while the contempt
authority is designed to protect the court and its operation, that during any
evaluation of alleged guru misconduct the court would also, as a secondary
factor, consider others who are also the victims of these persons, and evaluate
the harm done to the justice system as a whole –
all
its participants – to
establish the deleterious effect of OPCA guru activities. To me it seems only
appropriate that the shield that protects the court should extend to the people
who use its services, when faced by this parasitic industry of conmen, scam
artists, and grifters. The court and those who appear in it are inextricably
linked, and defence of their rights is a function necessary and inherent to the
superior inherent jurisdiction courts of the Commonwealth tradition.

v.         Conclusion – OPCA Guru Misconduct as Contempt

[
253
]

OPCA gurus promote and sell techniques that are
either intended to break or frustrate court processes, or which have
historically proven to impeded court function. I believe this is an instance of
public activity which is potentially criminal contempt of court.

[
254
]

The test identified in the appellate case law is
that a criminal contempt of court sanction is appropriate when an activity constitutes
a “clear and present danger”, “real and imminent harm or threat to justice”.
OPCA gurus sell and promote techniques that damage the court. The judiciary
regularly encounters litigants who attempt to apply these techniques. Only a small
fraction of those events are documented in reported case law. This is not
merely a theoretical issue, but one that is a regular and unwelcome event.

[
255
]

Thus, though what Mr. Fearn says likely would be
preposterous, absurd, and probably offensive to the average Canadian, he is one
of a community of like-minded persons. In their eyes Mr. Fearn’s “truths” are
very real. To permit the business of interfering with court processes to go unchallenged
only reinforces this community’s misguided, dystopian world perspective.

[
256
]

As far as I am aware Mr. Fearn does not sell or
otherwise commercially promote OPCA concepts. My exploration of this aspect of
the interaction between criminal court authority and OPCA schemes is intended
to help him and other like-minded persons to better understand the implications
of their beliefs and concepts, and assist the Crown identify what options exist
to respond to this unorthodox and troubling attack on the Canadian court
apparatus.

IV.       Conclusion

[
257
]

Mr. Fearn’s application is dismissed. As I said
in my oral reasons:

1.         the
Provincial Court proceeding is not stopped;

2.         Mr. Fearn is precluded from filing anything in the Court
of Queen’s Bench related to the Border Action, without first obtaining an Order
of this Court; and

3.         if the Crown wishes to stop Mr. Fearn from filing any
other application, it may apply to me under the
Judicature Act
, with
notice to Mr. Fearn.

[
258
]

I write these detailed reasons so that Mr. Fearn
may better appreciate why he has failed in this court. His application was in
the wrong forum and attempted to circumvent justice system procedures. His
arguments are not merely legally wrong, but often legally doltish. Mr. Fearn’s
litigation is vexatious and frivolous, he litigates without hope of success,
and thus logically only for the purpose of frustrating the courts and wasting
government resources.

[
259
]

While I felt this case probably merits costs, I
did not grant them in part due to the nature of his application, being a
challenge to a criminal proceeding in another Court. That said, I believe the
issue of costs should be spoken to in the future if Mr. Fearn advances a
further application or procedure that is equally frivolous, vexatious, or a
collateral attack on a sister court’s jurisdiction. Costs would have been an
unusual, even exceptional remedy. Now Mr. Fearn is warned that even in this
context his litigation approaches will have consequences.

[
260
]

Contempt of court is a mechanism to curb OPCA
misconduct that is directed to and interferes with court operation and
function. This response should be broad and meaningful. That reflects this
authority as an expression of the inherent jurisdiction of this Court. That
means that while freedom of expression is a value respected and protected both
under the common law and the
Charter
, that right does not extend to
speech and communication which is criminal, or is intended to or injures the
administration of justice and the rights of justice system participants.

[
261
]

At the closing of
Meads
, at para

730
, Associate Chief Justice Rooke observed that Mr. Meads was correct when he
said he had much to think about. The same now is true for Mr. Fearn.

[
262
]

This Court and the Alberta Provincial Court are
prepared to hear Mr. Fearn’s legitimate arguments and applications. He has
rights under law and the
Constitution
that will be protected. For
example, if he alleges mistreatment by the CBSA, then that may be basis for a
Charter

application. The law and courts exist to assist him, if he so chooses. It is
clear Mr. Fearn knows how to write court documents. He merely has to choose alternatives
that actually provide a potential benefit, rather than envisioning the vagaries
of a sovereign with no legal status, and no hope of success.
